# Fūjin: the stories first, then the spelling

You cannot weigh an accent without knowing what it carries. Here is what **Fūjin** has been carrying.

## The Stories That Carry the Name

**The Birth of the Wind Kami.** The wind kami are older than the name Fūjin.  In the Kojiki's birth-of-the-kami sequence, the wind god Shina-tsu-hiko (志那都比古) and his partner Shina-tsu-hime are born as Izanagi and Izanami take stock of the elemental kami of the new-made land; the Nihon Shoki preserves the lovelier etiology — Izanagi, looking out over the country he had made, found it wrapped in morning mist, breathed, and blew the fog away, and that first breath became the wind god.  The thunder kami have a harsher nativity: when the fire god Kagutsuchi burned his mother Izanami to death, Izanagi cut him down, and from the sword's blood were born the thunder gods, among them Takemikazuchi — born, like storm's own electricity, from the catastrophe of fire itself.

**The Cave and the Returning Winds.** When Amaterasu hid herself in the heavenly rock-cave (Ama-no-Iwato), the world did not merely lose its light — it lost its motion: the kami assembled in the dark, and the very winds of heaven stilled with everything else.  The ritual comedy by which the goddess was lured back — the cock, the mirror, Ame-no-Uzume's dance on an upturned tub — is therefore also a weather-myth: when the cave door opened, light returned with wind, rain, and the movement of all things (Kojiki; Aston's Nihongi). The medieval tradition that paired Fūjin with Raijin at temple gates read this old story into architecture: wind and thunder stand together at the threshold because both are signs that the hidden has come back out.

**Fūten, Guardian of the Directions.** In esoteric Buddhism the wind god is Fūten, one of the Twelve Devas (jūniten) who stand guard around the mandala, assigned in the Japanese tradition to the north-west.  He is the Vedic Vāyu carried east along the Silk Road — the Indian wind god appears among the outer guardians of the Womb-realm mandala — and Japan re-dressed him in the kami's leopard skin and gave him Raijin for a brother.  Temples fixed the pair in the national imagination: Kanō Tan'yū's wind-and-thunder paintings at Sanjūsangen-dō in Kyōto and Tawaraya Sōtatsu's celebrated Fūjin-Raijin folding screens at Kennin-ji turn two directional guardians into an eternal weather-front.

## And Here Is What the Spelling Preserves

Against those stories, the attestation: **風神**, as Kojiki (birth of the wind kami in the divine age) and Nihon Shoki (age of the gods; the Ama-no-Iwato episode) preserve it. The name means "Wind god".

The restoration keeps one feature the ASCII form *fujin* cannot show:

- **u → ū** — Long vowel: how long the vowel is held.

A storyteller pronouncing the name would restore every one of them by instinct. The file only writes down what the voice already knows.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Fūjin
- **ASCII form:** fujin
- **Meaning:** "Wind god"
- **Domain of influence:** Wind
- **Pantheon:** Japanese
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** 風神
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 163 of 546

## The Name Travels

Fūjin descends from the Chinese wind deity Fengshen, transmitted to Japan along with Buddhism and continental iconography.  He also resembles wind gods across Eurasia, from the Greek Boreas and the Vedic Vāta to the Central Asian wind demons depicted on Silk Road textiles.

## The Address It Earned

The temple of **Fūjin** stands at [/fujin/](/fujin/) — [lore](/fujin/lore/), [scholars](/fujin/scholars/), [patterns](/fujin/patterns/) — because a name carrying this much story deserves more than a parking page. What survives here cannot be shown in ASCII: a feature of the original that the fallback alphabet flattens. That is the Tier-1 test, and this name passes it without argument.

## The Sources Are Open

The myths above are retold from the temple's record; the primary voices are in the [Sacred Texts](/texts/): [Kojiki](/texts/kojiki/) and [Nihon Shoki](/texts/nihon-shoki/). Nothing in this file outranks them.
